item.title: AWS Network Firewall Adds Context-Aware Rules and Next Generation Policies
item.description:
AWS Network Firewall Adds Context-Aware Rules and Next Generation Policies

AWS Network Firewall has updated its capabilities to support context-aware rules, allowing you to match traffic based on the AWS resources that send and receive it rather than by their IP addresses. Alongside this, AWS has introduced Next Generation policies, which separate access control and threat protection into independent engines to help simplify firewall management and policy scaling.

🔍 Overview

Rules that match on IP addresses must keep up with every workload that scales out, is replaced, or moves. Short-lived workloads are the hardest to keep up with; for example, a VPC-attached AWS Lambda function can scale out and start sending traffic before an updated IP list reaches the firewall. Context-aware rules solve this issue by allowing you to filter a function’s traffic by the security group attached to it, or by naming a virtual private cloud (VPC), a subnet, or a transit gateway attachment.

🧩 How it works

Context-aware rules require transit gateway-attached firewalls and function by combining a control path and a data path:

  • The Control Path: A context store—which is a catalog of the AWS resources that can send and receive traffic through a transit gateway—tells the firewall which resources exist. You create this in AWS Network Manager and associate it with the transit gateway that your firewall uses.
  • The Data Path: The transit gateway adds the context of the sender (including its VPC, subnet, transit gateway attachment, and security groups) to each packet.
  • The Firewall Engine: The firewall receives these two paths, reads the context on each packet, and matches it against your configured rules. Source context works with every protocol, while destination context requires TCP-based rules because the firewall learns the receiving resource from return traffic.

Here is how context rules apply to specific AWS resources:

Resource Type Rule Application
Subnet or VPC Applies to each new resource that you launch in it.
Security Group Applies to each new resource whose network interface has that security group attached.
Transit Gateway Attachment Applies to traffic that enters through that attachment.

⚙️ Next Generation Policies

In a Classic policy, your access rules and threat rules run together in a single stateful engine and share one rule capacity. With Next Generation policies, access control and threat protection each get their own stateful engine in the same firewall, executed in sequence:

  1. Firewall Engine: This engine handles access control and is drop by default. Built on Suricata 8 firewall mode, it follows each connection through its entire flow (including the TCP handshake and TLS client hello) and evaluates rules along the way up to the application layer.
  2. IPS Engine: This engine manages threat protection and is pass by default. Traffic allowed by the firewall engine moves here, where the IPS engine checks it using AWS managed rule groups or custom rules that you write.

Because each engine has its own rule capacity, adding access rules does not take capacity away from threat protection. This design allows networking and security teams to work independently on their own configurations without risk of overwriting each other’s rules.

#AWS #NetworkFirewall #CloudSecurity #VPC #TransitGateway

Source: Introducing context-aware rules for AWS Network Firewall | Amazon Web Services Source: Introducing AWS Network Firewall Next Generation policy | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Private VPC Connectivity for Amazon Quick Enterprise Data Sources
item.description:
Private VPC Connectivity for Amazon Quick Enterprise Data Sources

Amazon Quick now supports private connections to on‑premises data sources, letting enterprises keep regulated data behind firewalls while still using AI‑powered search, analytics, and automation.

🔍 Overview

  • Amazon Quick is an AI‑powered workspace that brings search, analytics, research, and automation into a single conversational experience.
  • When enterprise data sits behind a corporate firewall or in a private on‑premises data center, there is no direct network path from AWS, even though the AI agents and dashboards in Amazon Quick can query virtually any data source.
  • Regulatory frameworks such as HIPAA, FedRAMP, and PCI‑DSS often mandate that sensitive data remain within controlled network boundaries.

🛠️ How it Works

  • Requires an existing AWS Direct Connect or Site‑to‑Site VPN linking the on‑premises environment to the VPC.
  • Configure VPC endpoints powered by AWS PrivateLink so Quick reaches private resources over the AWS backbone.
  • Layer security groups and VPC endpoint policies for defense in depth.
  • Data‑fetching traffic (when Quick reaches into your network) travels through the VPC connection, never over the public internet.

📊 Supported Data Sources

Source Type Example Databases Connection Method
On‑premises relational databases PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, and others Queried by Amazon Quick Sight through ENIs placed in the VPC (heaviest consumer of VPC connections)
Knowledge‑base source (VPC‑only) Amazon Redshift Supported VPC connection for Quick Index
Other knowledge sources (no VPC) Confluence, SharePoint, Box, Google Drive, OneDrive, Amazon S3 Cannot use a Quick VPC connection today (but S3 bucket access can be restricted via a VPC endpoint bucket policy)

⚙️ Automation Features with Private Connectivity

  • Quick Agents underpin all conversational interactions and can invoke action connectors directly; traffic to privately hosted MCP servers or internal APIs flows through the VPC connection.
  • Quick Flows handle repeatable tasks; they invoke action connectors, including MCP servers in the VPC.
  • Quick Automate handles complex, multi‑system orchestration with human‑in‑the‑loop; any workflow calling an internal API routes through the VPC path.
  • Quick Apps inherit the same VPC connectivity as Quick Sight and Flows for interactive web applications.
  • Quick Spaces organize content but do not initiate their own data connections.

🚀 Availability & Requirements

  • An active AWS account with an Amazon Quick Enterprise subscription (VPC connections require Enterprise edition).
  • An existing VPC in the AWS Region where Quick is deployed.
  • Direct Connect or Site‑to‑Site VPN already established.
  • Quick website VPC endpoints are not available in the AWS China Regions or the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Enables enterprises to keep regulated data within controlled network boundaries while still leveraging AI‑driven search, analytics, and automation.
  • Provides a private, AWS‑backbone path that avoids the public internet, meeting compliance mandates such as HIPAA, FedRAMP, and PCI‑DSS.
  • Offers defense‑in‑depth security through VPC endpoint policies and security groups.

#AWS #AmazonQuick #VPC #EnterpriseAI #DataSecurity

Source: Securing Quick access from corporate networks with AWS PrivateLink | Amazon Web Services
